Explores how EU chemicals can become both competitive and low-emissions. 
First finds that the EU cannot continue to compete on price for commodity products, even if it scraps its climate policies all together. Only way to remain competitive is by moving beyond price-based competition. Instead, profitability must be ensured through politically shaped markets that provide green premium for environmental and circular attributes of products.

Pieter has made a summary of the report see here: https://eea1.sharepoint.com/:p:/r/teams/SecretariattotheAdvisoryBoard/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BEC8A6BCD-5D08-4693-877D-FB57692A9153%7D&file=CEFIC%20Carbon%20managers.pptx&action=edit&mobileredirect=true

Provides overview of main decarbonisation options including their reduction potential and marginal abatement costs for steel. Also includes overview of recent transition pathways in which these different options are combined to different extents.

Provides overview of main decarbonisation options including their reduction potential and marginal abatement costs for ammonia production. Also includes overview of recent transition pathways in which these different options are combined to different extents.

Provides overview of main decarbonisation options including their reduction potential and marginal abatement costs for cement. Also includes overview of recent transition pathways in which these different options are combined to different extents.

The Commission's country level recommendations touch on several aspects of industrial decarbonisation from access to finance and business environment, skills and infrastructure, economic security and strategic capacity, innovation and technology. Worthwhile cross-checking before we say that EC does nothing on any of these as it may be that it exercises its soft power through this process.
